title: The Difficult 1-on-1
subtitle: Telling someone their performance is below the bar
description: You are a manager. Your direct report Aryan has missed targets for two quarters. Today is the 1-on-1 where you must tell him clearly that his performance is below the bar — with empathy, honesty, and a path forward.
learning_objectives: Deliver a difficult performance message with clarity and compassion
Balance honesty with psychological safety in a hard conversation
Create a concrete improvement plan that the employee owns
reflection_prompt: What part of this conversation would you find hardest to do in real life, and why?
coaching_moment: The hardest conversations are the ones that matter most. Delaying them is the cruelest thing a manager can do.

rounds.title: Setting the Tone
rounds.situation: Aryan walks in looking a bit nervous. You have 30 minutes. How do you open the conversation?
rounds.story: The first 60 seconds of a difficult conversation set the psychological safety for everything that follows.
rounds.coaching_moment: Opening with appreciation before hard feedback is not softening — it is establishing that this is a conversation, not an ambush.

choices.label: Open with data: 'Aryan, you have missed Q2 and Q3 targets. We need to talk.'
choices.description: Direct and clear, but may put Aryan immediately on the defensive.
choices.consequence_hint: He may shut down before you can have a real conversation.
choices.feedback: Aryan's shoulders tense up before you've even finished the sentence. He nods stiffly and says 'Okay' in a flat voice. The room goes quiet. You've established clarity fast, but you can feel the temperature drop — the next 29 minutes will be harder to steer toward anything collaborative.

choices.label: Start with genuine appreciation: 'I want to start by saying I value having you on the team. That is exactly why I need to be honest with you today.'
choices.description: Builds psychological safety before the hard message.
choices.consequence_hint: He is more likely to hear what comes next with an open mind.
choices.feedback: Aryan's posture softens slightly. 'Okay,' he says, sitting forward instead of back. The appreciation didn't erase his nerves, but it bought you something valuable: he's listening to understand, not just waiting to defend himself.

choices.label: Ask how he thinks things are going first.
choices.description: Let him self-assess before you share your view.
choices.consequence_hint: Gives you insight into his self-awareness and saves the feedback from feeling like an attack.
choices.feedback: Aryan hesitates, then admits: 'Honestly? Not great. I know Q2 and Q3 weren't where they needed to be.' He beat you to the hard part — which tells you he's more self-aware than you expected, and gives you a real opening instead of a confrontation.

rounds.title: Delivering the Message
rounds.situation: Aryan admits things have been 'a bit slow' but does not acknowledge the severity. It is time to name the reality clearly.
rounds.story: Clarity is a form of kindness. Vague feedback is a gift that keeps harming.
rounds.coaching_moment: Use the SBI model: Situation, Behaviour, Impact. Specific, observable, not personal.

decision_data.title: Why This Matters to the Org

rows.label: Aryan's team share of your total pipeline
Org-wide Q3 revenue miss so far
Aryan's direct reports watching this outcome

choices.label: Be direct: 'Aryan, to be clear — your performance is below the bar we need. This is not a minor gap.'
choices.description: Specific and honest without attacking his character.
choices.consequence_hint: This lands clearly. Aryan goes quiet but stays in the room.
choices.feedback: 'Below the bar' lands like a physical weight. Aryan doesn't argue — he just says 'I understand' quietly. There's no ambiguity left in the room, which is exactly what you needed, even if the silence that follows is uncomfortable.

choices.label: Soften it: 'Look, no one is perfect. You just need to try a bit harder.'
choices.description: Avoids discomfort but fails to communicate the real stakes.
choices.consequence_hint: Aryan leaves not understanding he is at risk.
choices.feedback: Aryan actually smiles a little, relieved. 'Yeah, I'll pick it up.' He walks out of this round believing it was a minor course-correction — not a conversation about his job being at risk. You've bought comfort now at the cost of an honest reckoning later.

choices.label: Name the business impact: 'Your team's pipeline is 40% of mine. When it misses, the whole org feels it.'
choices.description: Connects the feedback to something bigger than individual numbers.
choices.consequence_hint: Aryan looks shaken but not humiliated. He understands why this matters.
choices.feedback: Aryan's eyes widen slightly at the 40% figure — he hadn't framed his own numbers at that scale before. 'I didn't realize it was that connected,' he says. The stakes just became real to him in a way that feels motivating rather than crushing.

rounds.title: Listening to His Side
rounds.situation: Aryan says: 'I have been struggling since the team restructure. I did not get the training on the new CRM. I probably should have said something sooner.'
rounds.story: Performance gaps often have structural causes. A good manager separates what is the employee's issue from what is theirs.
rounds.coaching_moment: Listening here is not just compassionate — it is strategically essential. You cannot fix what you do not understand.

rows.label: Team members who got CRM training

choices.label: Acknowledge: 'That context matters. I should have made sure you had that training — that is on me.'
choices.description: Takes accountability for your part without excusing the performance gap.
choices.consequence_hint: Aryan visibly relaxes. The conversation becomes collaborative.
choices.feedback: Aryan exhales, like he'd been bracing for you to dismiss this. 'I appreciate you saying that,' he says. The conversation shifts from 'you versus me' to 'us versus the problem' — the single biggest turn this meeting could take.

choices.label: Push back: 'The restructure was 6 months ago. Why are you telling me this now?'
choices.description: Valid question but the timing is defensive.
choices.consequence_hint: Aryan shuts down. He feels blamed rather than heard.
choices.feedback: Aryan's face closes off. 'I don't know, I guess I thought I could handle it,' he mutters, looking at the table. The question was fair, but the delivery reads as an accusation — he's now more focused on defending the timing than solving the real problem.

choices.label: Note it and move on: 'Okay, I hear that. Let us focus on what we do from here.'
choices.description: Keeps momentum but may feel like you dismissed his concern.
choices.consequence_hint: Aryan nods but the moment of real connection was missed.
choices.feedback: Aryan nods and says 'Sure, that's fine' — but something in his tone suggests he expected more acknowledgment than a quick pivot. You kept the meeting moving, but a small trust-building opportunity slipped by unclaimed.

rounds.title: Building the Plan
rounds.situation: The hard part is over. Now you need to leave with a concrete plan. Aryan asks: 'What do you need from me in the next 90 days?'
rounds.story: A difficult conversation without a plan is just pain with no purpose.
rounds.coaching_moment: The best performance plans are owned by the employee, not handed down. Ask before you tell.

choices.label: Hand him a written PIP with specific metrics.
choices.description: Clear and formal, but Aryan may feel it was pre-decided before the conversation.
choices.consequence_hint: He reads it carefully. Clarity is high but ownership is low.
choices.feedback: Aryan reads the document line by line, nodding at each metric. It's unambiguous — but he's reading it the way you'd read a legal notice, not a plan you built together. He'll follow it, but you're not sure yet if he believes in it.

choices.label: Ask him: 'What do you think a fair 90-day goal looks like? Let us build this together.'
choices.description: Builds ownership by letting him co-author his own recovery plan.
choices.consequence_hint: Aryan suggests targets. They are slightly lower than yours but he writes them down himself.
choices.feedback: Aryan thinks for a moment, then proposes 100% coverage by week 8 and 120% by end of Q4 — close to what you'd have asked for, but in his own words. He writes it down himself. A plan someone builds is a plan they defend.

choices.label: Tell him the outcome first: 'I need pipeline coverage at 120% by Q4. How you get there is your call.'
choices.description: Sets the north star but gives him agency on the path.
choices.consequence_hint: Aryan nods. He looks energised rather than defeated.
choices.feedback: '120%, got it,' Aryan says, already thinking out loud about which accounts he'd prioritize. Giving him the destination but not the route seems to switch something on — he leaves this round talking tactics, not excuses.

rounds.title: Closing the Conversation
rounds.situation: You are at the end of the meeting. Aryan is quiet, processing. He asks: 'Am I at risk of losing my job?'
rounds.story: Honesty at the close of a hard conversation determines whether the person leaves with clarity or anxiety.
rounds.coaching_moment: Ambiguity here is not kindness — it is a slow form of cruelty. Say clearly what is true.

rows.label: Question Aryan just asked directly
rows.value: "Am I at risk of losing my job?"

choices.label: Be honest: 'If the 90-day plan does not show movement, yes — your role is at risk. I want you to know the stakes.'
choices.description: Hard to say but essential. He deserves to know.
choices.consequence_hint: Aryan looks serious. He thanks you for being straight with him.
choices.feedback: Aryan is quiet for a moment, then says: 'Okay. Thank you for telling me straight.' He leaves the room with a clear picture of exactly what's at stake and exactly what he controls — which, hard as it was to say, is the most respectful thing you could have given him.

choices.label: Reassure: 'You are fine. Just keep improving.'
choices.description: Avoids a difficult moment but leaves him without accurate information.
choices.consequence_hint: Aryan leaves relieved but not clear on the stakes. The 90-day deadline may come as a shock.
choices.feedback: Aryan's shoulders drop with relief. 'Okay, good, thanks.' He walks out believing this was a routine check-in — not the last chance you actually meant it to be. If day 90 arrives without progress, this moment of comfort will look, in hindsight, like the conversation you avoided having.

choices.label: Restate the plan as the closing anchor: 'Focus on the 90-day targets. Let us meet again in 30 days to check in.'
choices.description: Redirects to the plan without fully answering the question.
choices.consequence_hint: He knows you did not fully answer, but the structure is comforting.
choices.feedback: 'Sounds good,' Aryan says, though you both know he asked a yes-or-no question and got a plan instead. The 30-day check-in gives him something concrete to hold onto, even if the direct question is still quietly unanswered.

glossary_terms.definition: Situation, Behaviour, Impact — a framework for delivering specific, non-personal feedback
A formal document outlining performance gaps and the steps needed to address them within a timeframe
The belief that one can speak up, make mistakes, or give feedback without fear of punishment
